name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at your accounting firm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A repair shop will often send a warranty credit without the original invoice, so I look through the account until I can explain the gap. I prepare the accounts and tax return, then the partner checks the final file. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification; I enjoy getting a messy ledger to balance, but the owner’s last-minute paperwork can keep me after closing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Kiran does freelance print design, and our children Ada and Leo are both school age. We have a mortgage, but I earn high pay for this accounting role and have about thirteen months of expenses saved, with plenty of similar firms nearby. I have never used AI, and I prefer the spreadsheet and the original invoice over an answer I cannot trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repair shops would still bring me warranty credits after the month closes. A little sorting help would not change the questions I ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office that a receipt sorter is acceptable if we can see how it reached a total. I would keep a named accountant on every return we send out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, our work and money feel safe here: my pay is high, we have around thirteen months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of firms nearby. My partner Kiran has design clients, and the mortgage is covered by our present income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reconciling repair-shop warranty credits with original invoices and preparing returns under the current review rule. I would put a fixed seventy from each monthly wage toward extra mortgage principal if the lender confirms there is no early-payment fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household bills in this picture. A warranty credit with no matching invoice would still keep me at work late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool, and I would want my manager Rosa to show me a checked example first. Until the firm sets a traceable process, I would keep the spreadsheet I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay the loan early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller balance gives our children more room later without using the thirteen-month emergency reserve. I would use new money from salary only if the lender does not charge us for it.

say: I would accept receipt sorting only with **traceable totals** from the original repair-shop invoices.
I would keep a **named accountant** responsible for every tax return the firm sends.
think: Our **thirteen-month reserve** and high pay keep the mortgage secure.
Plenty of local firms offer **similar accounting work**.
do: Keep reconciling **warranty credits** against original repair-shop invoices before each return.
Pay **seventy monthly** from wages toward mortgage principal only if the lender charges no fee.
feel: I feel **calm** about our current income.
S0.quote: A warranty credit with no matching invoice would still keep me at work late.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and insists on an explainable process before changing a live return.
Her extra mortgage payment uses **new salary cash** only if no lender fee applies.

steps.text: Keep reconciling repair-shop warranty credits with original invoices
Pay seventy monthly from salary toward mortgage principal only if penalty-free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first checks on my desk could move into a program. Kiran’s design drafts might change even faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that the firm should show what the software misses and give staff notice before changing hours. I would also ask our association to put the named signer into a written policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my own checking hours could fall, and Kiran’s freelance design bookings could shrink as AI writes and draws more. Our year of savings gives us time, but two reduced wages would upset the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I would bring our error log and staffing sheet to the accountants’ association meeting and ask for written notice. If my paid hours fall in the first year, I would apply only to posted accountant vacancies with written wages, hours, and a start date covering our mortgage; I would keep my current work while any pay remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because both our incomes could shrink. A strong reserve buys time to choose a job, not proof that a client will keep paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the firm’s AI system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a live client file. I have never used AI, and I would watch a paid, supervised demonstration only after Rosa shows us an error test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kiran do if bookings slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Kiran would ask existing clients for firm bookings before taking on new debt. We would count only signed design work in the household budget.

I would ask for a **named signer** in the firm’s written policy.

Apply for **posted accountant jobs** after hour cuts only with written mortgage-covering terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about both household incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is close enough to be a household budget, not a career theory. Both a tax desk and a design screen face AGI in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm owes clients a named signer and staff a clear notice period when AGI does accounts in 2028. I would tell family that robots around 2031 are later and do not delay our desk risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my accounting post to go, and Kiran may lose most design bookings at the same time. Our thirteen-month reserve is substantial, but two missing incomes and a mortgage would use it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would pause the planned kitchen extension and put its monthly budget into a separate cash reserve, while asking the association to negotiate severance. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I would take a posted repair-shop accounts role only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering the mortgage; I would keep our current salary until a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect both kinds of screen work to lose income. I have cash and a plan, but not a signed job on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a repair-shop accounts job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the warranty records and can speak to owners, but AGI may reach those accounts too. I would treat a paid opening as a bridge, not say it solves the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not while we have savings and can still work. I would ask my brother Dev about school pickup only if an actual new shift made the current arrangement impossible.

S2.quote: Our thirteen-month reserve is substantial, but two missing incomes and a mortgage would use it quickly.
fieldNote: She identifies **simultaneous desk exposure** for accounting and freelance design in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us lower the loan before both kinds of desk work change. I could learn the client side without buying a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to seek paid practice on disputed returns and notice before 2031. AGI reaches accounting and design screens then, while robots around 2034 reach hands-on tasks later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think my checking post could disappear, and Kiran’s design clients could leave too. Five years gives us time to reduce the mortgage principal and see whether the firm funds a real client role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Rosa to pair me with a senior accountant on one paid client objection each quarter and work through the case only if she assigns paid time. I would make an extra seventy mortgage payment from each monthly wage if the lender confirms it is penalty-free; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted client representative job only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering the loan and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual loss of both incomes, but five years allows measured work and loan payments. I would keep my present wage if no funded client place appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Rosa cannot give you paid cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the professional body’s free case notes while continuing the repair-shop returns that pay me. I would not spend the reserve on a course just because the clock is ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted job with a signed wage and agreed start date that fit school pickup. Plenty of firms are nearby, but I would not leave a good wage for a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would take our children toward adult jobs. I would still want to keep the house steady while I learn what clients value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers the firm can teach real tax judgment and keep named sign-off before AGI reaches accounts in 2036. Robots around 2039 come later for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect basic return fees to fall eventually, and Kiran’s design work has the same 2036 desk date. Our high pay and year-plus reserve make the next few years secure enough to pay down the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reconciling the current warranty accounts and make an extra seventy principal payment from each monthly wage if the lender confirms no penalty. I would join paid client objections only if Rosa assigns them; if my accounting role contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted client role only with signed wage, hours, and start date covering our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant double desk shock, but our current bills are covered. Ten years lets us lower fixed costs without selling the house in fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a rule at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a named human signer and a notice period before any automated cut. I would take the error list to the professional association with colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ada and Leo to avoid office work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Ada and Leo to learn a skill someone can check and explain. I would not pick their careers from one frightening forecast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both my accounting wage and Kiran’s design bookings could shrink at once. Severance agreed in advance, paid supervised client work, and a real posted job with written pay would help. I would use cash for the mortgage before asking family for money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs an automated return when a repair shop gets a penalty notice. A perfect spreadsheet can still leave someone at the counter with a real bill. I want one person named on the answer.

headlineQuote: A perfect spreadsheet can still leave someone at the counter with a real bill.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles repair-shop accounts.
She has **high pay**, thirteen months saved, a freelance-designer partner, two school-age children, and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI**, prefers original invoices, and lives near plenty of other firms.
A fast **2028** shock threatens both desk-based incomes, despite the strong reserve.
Longer warning lets her use **new wages** to reduce mortgage principal and learn client objections on paid time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink her accountant wage and Kiran’s freelance design income together.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **agreed severance**, paid supervised client work, and a posted role with written pay.
